definition: Rude and openly disrespectful, especially toward someone in charge.
example: Her insolent shrug when the chef asked her to clean the stove got her moved to dish duty.
nuance: Insolent suggests scorn for authority; impudent and cheeky can describe bold rudeness that is milder or even playful.
prompt: A referee calls a foul against a player during a youth soccer match.
options: The player gave the referee an insolent smirk and walked away mid-sentence.
The insolent club could no longer afford new uniforms or bus trips to away games.
The insolent player thanked the referee and calmly accepted the call.
The insolent goalkeeper lounged on the bench, too sluggish to bother warming up.
reasons: A mocking look and walking off while an official is talking show contempt for authority.
Running out of money describes being insolvent, a look-alike word.
Accepting a ruling politely is respectful, which is the reverse of this word.
Laziness and lack of energy describe indolence, not rudeness.

practice.prompt: A librarian asks a teenager to lower his voice in the reading room.
options: The insolent teenager spoke so softly that nobody at the next table could hear him.
The teenager answered with an insolent remark about minding her own business.
The insolent teenager apologized at once and whispered for the rest of the afternoon.
The insolent teenager owed so many late fees that his library card was frozen.
reasons: Speaking quietly is about volume and has nothing to do with disrespect.
A rude comeback to a reasonable request shows open scorn for the librarian's authority.
Apologizing and doing as asked show respect, the opposite of what the word means.
Debts a person cannot pay suggest insolvent, a word that only sounds similar.
